name: PT Pyridam Farma Tbk

frontmatter.title: Pyridam Farma — a real CDMO business behind an unpayable balance sheet
frontmatter.summary: Revenue has doubled twice on the Probiotec and Ethica acquisitions and EBITDA is now positive, but cash interest exceeds EBITDA and debt is several times any defensible enterprise value. The equity survives only as an option on a margin step-change or a trade sale. We initiate at SELL with a target of Rp32.
thesis: Revenue tripled in two years and the operating business is real; restated FY2025 EBITDA is IDR75.5bn, not the negative figure in the data pack.
Finance cost of IDR325.9bn in FY2025 and IDR322.4bn in nine months of 2026 exceeds EBITDA, so operating progress accrues to lenders, not shareholders.

Our base-case DCF gives an enterprise value of IDR1,077.6bn against net debt of IDR4,739.6bn at the last audited year-end and IDR4,159.0bn plus IDR1,335.0bn less cash of IDR126.1bn at 30 September 2026; the equity is worth zero on operating value.

The market pays IDR1,325.9bn of equity value and 17.7x FY2027E EBITDA, on FY2027E net debt and before the investment credit — the higher of the two bases — for a contract manufacturer whose EBITDA converts to very little free cash.
Only the bull case, in which margins reach formulator-peer levels, restores equity value; it carries a real but minority probability and is the whole of our target.

catalysts.event: Audited FY2026 results — first full year with the Probiotec assets and the current cost base
First coupon on the Phase II bond and the 2027 maturity wall; refinancing terms
End of the controlling shareholder's financial support letter

blocks.text: We initiate on PT Pyridam Farma at SELL with a target of Rp32, against a price of Rp118, an expected return of -72.6%. The company has done what management promised on the top line: net revenue rose from IDR702.0bn in FY2023 to IDR1,920.0bn in FY2024 and IDR2,760.0bn in FY2025, and the first nine months of 2026 grew again on the same period, with gross margin of 21.1% in FY2025 and higher in 2026 [S4][S8]. EBITDA has followed: IDR239.9bn in the first nine months of 2026 against almost nothing a year earlier [S11].

That is the bull case, and we take it seriously. What kills the equity is the capital structure underneath it. Finance cost was IDR322.4bn in the first nine months of 2026 against IDR239.0bn a year earlier [S4], on interest-bearing debt of IDR4,841.4bn at the last audited balance sheet and IDR4,159.0bn of bank and bond borrowings plus IDR1,335.0bn of lease liabilities at the interim [S16][S14]. EBITDA covers less than three quarters of interest, so the group still consumes cash and funds the gap with more debt: net debt was IDR4,739.6bn at the FY2025 accounts, IDR4,159.0bn plus IDR1,335.0bn less cash of IDR126.1bn at 30 September 2026, and IDR6,636.3bn on our FY2030E balance sheet.

Our valuation does not need a bearish operating view to reach zero. On the base case the discounted cash flow gives an enterprise value of IDR1,077.6bn; subtract net debt and minorities and add investments and nothing is left for shareholders, so the equity is worth zero on operating value. The price of Rp118 capitalises the group at IDR1,325.9bn and puts the enterprise at 17.7x our FY2027E EBITDA of IDR399.3bn, measured on FY2027E net debt and before the investment credit; on the printed 30 September 2026 bridge the same arithmetic gives a multiple about three quarters of a turn lower, so the figure quoted here is the higher of the two. Even that is a multiple for a contract manufacturer whose EBITDA barely converts to free cash at the current cost of capital.

The gap between that multiple and what the cash flows support is the whole call. It is not a forecast that the business fails: revenue grows every year in our base case, EBITDA rises from IDR334.0bn to IDR590.3bn, and gross margin improves. It is that the enterprise value those cash flows support is smaller than the debt, and the equity is a residual claim on an enterprise that is worth less than what it owes.

Pyridam Farma is one of the older Indonesian pharmaceutical manufacturers, and for most of its listed history it was a small domestic formulator selling through distributors. The transformation into a contract development and manufacturing business is recent, and it changed the character of the company: contract work is capital intensive, priced partly in hard currency for export clients, and dependent on a handful of large customers rather than on a broad domestic brand portfolio. Investors who remember the earlier business are valuing a different company.

PYFA manufactures pharmaceutical products and sells contract development and manufacturing services. The group describes its offer as end-to-end: formulation and development, dossier compilation and regulatory work including marketing-authorisation-holder services, manufacturing across a wide range of dosage forms, and logistics and marketing support for partners [S6]. Manufacturing runs on two country platforms, Indonesia and Australia, and covers tablets, capsules, granules, effervescents, syrups, injectables in ampoules and vials, creams, ointments and sprays [S6].

The group is a collection of acquired assets rather than a single plant. PT Holi Pharma was acquired in December 2021, PT Ethica Industri Farmasi in July 2022, and Probiotec Pty Ltd indirectly through Pyfa Australia Pty Ltd in June 2024; the group also holds Pyfa Health Singapore, PT Pyfa Aetheria Indonesia, PT Pyfa Investama Indonesia, PT Pyfa Sehat Indonesia and PT Medika Inovasi Nusantara, the last established in February 2025 [S7]. The step-up in revenue from IDR702.0bn to IDR2,760.0bn is largely the consolidation of those businesses rather than organic growth in the legacy formulation book [S8][S10].

The controlling shareholder is Rejuve Global Investment Pte Ltd, which is controlled by Lee Ee Ling [S7]. Rejuve held 60.5% of the register at 30 June 2026 and public holders below five per cent held 34.5% [S15]; the exchange's free-float measure is 29.6% because it nets the strategic holdings inside the register, and that traded float is the figure we use for the liquidity premium in the valuation section [S0]. The shares that trade are therefore a minority of the capital and the controlling block can determine any equity raise or related-party transaction. Management presents the company as an Asia-Pacific CDMO platform bidding for multinational and large domestic contracts, not as a branded generics house [S8].

Segment disclosure in the pack is thin: the company reports a pharmaceutical products, esthetic and toll manufacturing segment alongside a medical equipment segment, and we could not archive a filing that breaks out CDMO revenue separately [S0]. That is a genuine information gap. Management commentary says CDMO and toll manufacturing have been the growth engine for two consecutive years [S8], but we cannot size CDMO as a share of revenue or its standalone margin, which is why our forecast works at the group level.

The workforce is small for the revenue base: 2,341.0 employees across the group [S0], which is consistent with a manufacturing model that runs a few large sites rather than a distributed sales organisation. That is an advantage while volumes rise, because incremental revenue carries little incremental headcount, and a risk if a single site loses a client or a certification, because there is no second line of capacity in the same country to absorb the work. We treat site concentration as an operating risk rather than a financial one, but it reinforces why we do not pay a quality multiple for this business.

The relevant market is pharmaceutical contract manufacturing, not the Indonesian domestic drug market. Management cites a global CDMO market of roughly a quarter of a trillion US dollars in 2026, projected to reach about half a trillion by 2035, growing at a high single-digit to low double-digit compound rate, with Asia-Pacific the fastest-growing region [S8]. Those projections are the company's own framing of its opportunity and we treat them as context rather than as a forecast input.

The structural driver is real: global pharmaceutical groups continue to outsource manufacturing and, increasingly, development and regulatory work, which favours contract manufacturers with approved sites in more than one jurisdiction [S8]. PYFA's proposition rests on exactly that — an Indonesian cost base plus an Australian regulatory footprint via Probiotec, selling regulatory and dossier services alongside capacity [S6][S7]. The moat, if there is one, is switching cost: once a client's product is registered against a specific site and dossier, moving it is slow and expensive.

Against that, the group is a challenger, not a leader. The global CDMO field is dominated by far larger players with deeper technical benches and investment-grade balance sheets, and Indonesian contract manufacturing is fragmented and price-competitive. PYFA's own scale is small: IDR3,243.0bn of forecast revenue this year across two countries [S0]. Nothing in the material we archived shows a widening technical advantage, a proprietary platform or a customer relationship that a competitor could not replicate with capital.

Five forces work against the equity rather than the business. Buyer power is high because contract manufacturing is tendered and clients multi-source; supplier power is moderate; the threat of new capacity is high in Indonesia, where several groups hold idle formulation capacity; rivalry is intense and price-led. The one force that helps is switching cost after registration, and it protects revenue more than it protects margin. We size the group as a price-taker in its domestic work and a challenger in export contract work, which is the combination that produces a mid-teens gross margin rather than the high-twenties margin of a branded formulator [S4][S8].

Two external influences matter most. The first is the rupiah: the group reports in rupiah but earns part of its revenue in Australian and US dollars from export contract work, so a weaker rupiah helps the top line while it raises the local-currency cost of servicing dollar-linked debt [S0]. The second is Indonesian drug pricing and procurement policy, which constrains what domestic formulation work can earn and pushes the group toward export contract manufacturing as the higher-return activity [S8].

The result is a business with a defensible revenue base but no pricing power. That is why we model gross margin holding near the current level and improving only with volume absorption, and why we do not extrapolate the industry's headline growth into PYFA's margins [S4][S8].

The peer frame is instructive. The larger Indonesian healthcare names carry branded portfolios, distribution reach and net cash, and their margins reflect pricing power that PYFA does not have; the state-owned pharma names carry restructuring risk of a different kind. PYFA sits in neither camp: it is a contract manufacturer with a leveraged balance sheet, which means it should trade on enterprise value and cash flow rather than on a franchise multiple. Reading the peer reports only as a frame, the common thread is that Indonesian pharma margins are under pressure and that balance-sheet quality is what separates the names that can defend a rating from those that cannot [S0][S4].

Revenue history is a story of acquisitions, not compounding. Net revenue was IDR715.4bn in FY2022, IDR702.0bn in FY2023, IDR1,920.0bn in FY2024 and IDR2,760.0bn in FY2025, the last rise of 43.8% driven by a full year of Probiotec and by CDMO volume, with gross margin of 21.1% [S8][S10]. The first nine months of 2026 show net revenue of IDR2,410.0bn, gross profit of IDR542.8bn and a gross margin a little above the full-year 2025 level, up on the prior year because higher production volume spread the fixed cost base [S4].

Operating leverage is starting to appear. The nine-month operating result was a loss of IDR12.8bn, against a loss of IDR150.7bn a year earlier, on general and administrative expense of IDR337.4bn [S4]. Management's own EBITDA measure was IDR239.9bn for the nine months, against almost nil a year before, with depreciation and amortisation of IDR252.7bn, mostly on the assets acquired with Probiotec [S11].

The data pack is wrong on the depreciation line, and we restate it. Its D&A charge is a fraction of the audited figure, so its FY2025 EBITDA is negative; the audited accounts show D&A of IDR292.7bn (FY2024: IDR179.3bn), an operating result of IDR-217.2bn (FY2024: IDR-106.9bn) and finance cost of IDR325.9bn (FY2024: IDR226.0bn) [S16]. On the filing's numbers FY2025 EBITDA was positive at IDR75.5bn and FY2024 was IDR72.4bn. The pack builds EBITDA from a direct-method cash-flow statement, which is why its depreciation charge is understated and its EBITDA carries the wrong sign; the audited income statement is authoritative and history is restated line by line [S16].

Below the operating line the picture is dominated by debt service. Finance cost was IDR322.4bn in the first nine months of 2026 against IDR239.0bn a year earlier [S4], with the net loss narrowing to IDR338.7bn [S11] because of a smaller non-operating charge rather than because interest fell. Pre-tax loss was IDR-530.9bn in FY2025 and our forecast keeps the group loss-making at the net line through the forecast period: IDR-433.3bn this year and still IDR-384.6bn by FY2030 [S0].

Our forecast is built from the run-rate, not from the plan. We grow revenue 17.5% this year to IDR3,243.0bn, reflecting the nine-month rate and a normal fourth quarter, then fade growth toward single digits by FY2030 as CDMO capacity is absorbed [S4][S8]. Gross margin is held at about the current level and improved only with absorption; total operating expense, including D&A, falls as a share of revenue toward a fifth, which is the single most important operating assumption in the model. On that build, EBITDA reaches IDR334.0bn this year and IDR590.3bn in FY2030, an EBITDA margin of 12.0%.

Cash generation does not follow. Capex was IDR168.5bn in FY2025, and we hold it near that share of revenue before converging it toward the D&A charge by the end of the forecast, because a company cannot depreciate assets above reinvestment for ever. Interest and working capital absorb the rest: free cash flow to the firm is thin, and net debt rises to IDR6,636.3bn by FY2030 under our funding path [S14]. Working capital is the quiet risk — operating working capital was IDR621.5bn, about a fifth of revenue, carried largely in receivables from the acquired businesses [S0].

The debt is the part of the balance sheet that decides the equity. Interest-bearing debt was IDR4,841.4bn at 31 December 2025 — bank loans, bonds and lease liabilities [S16] — and IDR4,159.0bn of bank and bond borrowings plus IDR1,335.0bn of lease liabilities at 30 September 2026 [S14]. Against cash of IDR126.1bn at the interim, the same measure gives net debt of IDR4,739.6bn at the last audited year-end and the sum of those interim components at 30 September. The definition matters: the filing's own gearing note measures borrowings excluding lease liabilities, which is why its reported debt-to-equity ratio looks lower than ours [S14]; we include leases because EBITDA is struck before lease depreciation and interest, so the leases are a financing claim on the same earnings. Interest cover is below one times on an EBITDA basis. The group discloses that it did not meet the debt-service-coverage and debt-to-equity covenants at either 31 December 2025 or 30 September 2026, and no waiver is disclosed [S14]; management states its belief that this will not affect the status of the facilities. A company in that position does not control its own destiny: the lender sets the terms on which the operating improvement is retained. The funding mix says the same thing: interest-bearing borrowings rose by four-fifths of the total increase in liabilities over the first nine months of 2026, with the remainder in other payables and accruals, so debt rather than stretched trade credit is what carries the cash deficit [S14]. Our forecast net debt moves with the modelled cash deficit, not with the filed balance sheet, and the reconciliation is worth stating because it explains the whole gap a reader will find between the two. Over the nine months to 30 September 2026 operating activities used IDR335.9bn of cash and investing activities IDR65.9bn, and on top of that cash deficit the group added IDR35.6bn of new lease liabilities, IDR55.2bn of non-cash lease accretion and IDR139.4bn of foreign-currency translation to its lease balance [S14]. Those additions raise debt without passing through the cash-flow statement, which is why the filed measure is IDR4,159.0bn of borrowings plus IDR1,335.0bn of leases less cash of IDR126.1bn. Our forecast moves with the cash deficit alone, because the template's debt line carries no non-cash accretion, so FY2026E net debt of IDR5,128.6bn sits below the filed September figure. No fourth-quarter repayment is assumed anywhere in the model: the shortfall is the omitted accretion, it understates leverage rather than flattering it, and the valuation bridge — the number the target actually rests on — is struck entirely at the filed 30 September balance sheet.

Earnings-quality flags from our screen are as follows. On the accruals test the group is not manipulating earnings upward — it reports large losses and the accrual gap is modest — but cash conversion is unambiguously poor: operating cash flow is negative and the nine-month figures show no inflection [S16]. The financial statements carry an unmodified audit opinion, with goodwill of 27.9% of consolidated assets flagged as a key audit matter [S16]; that is the asset most at risk if the CDMO case disappoints. The company does not capitalise development costs to flatter the profit line and pays no dividend. Against those, the balance sheet has no slack at all: the covenant breach is disclosed, no waiver is in the filings and the group relies on a support letter from its controlling shareholder to keep trading [S14].

We value PYFA on a discounted cash flow to the firm. A price-to-earnings approach is meaningless here because the group is loss-making through the forecast, pays no dividend and has no positive trailing earnings; an EV/EBITDA cross-check on trailing EBITDA is negative on the data pack and only IDR75.5bn restated [S16]. We therefore give the DCF the whole weight and disclose the multiple test as a cross-check rather than a method. That is the right method set for a leveraged, capital-intensive contract manufacturer: value belongs to the enterprise, and the split between debt and equity is the argument.

The discount rate is at the bottom of the house band for Indonesian names, not in the middle of it. The build starts from a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4% less the 1.6% sovereign default spread, applies a relevered beta of 1.8x to the sum of a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5%, and adds our 3.0% small-cap premium, giving a cost of equity of 20.8% and a WACC of 11.9% [S0]. The spread is subtracted because the rupiah government yield already carries the sovereign default risk, so charging that risk again inside the equity premium would double-count it; the beta multiplication applies to the whole equity premium, which is why the components do not simply add to the cost of equity. The 3.0% small-cap premium reflects a market capitalisation of IDR1,325.9bn and a free float of 29.6% on the exchange's registry measure, which nets the strategic holdings that sit inside the shareholder register described in the governance section; it is the traded float, not the public shareholding, that sets the liquidity premium. Relevering is capped at a debt-to-equity ratio of 2.0x, which is short of the company's actual gearing, so the beta is understated if anything. A WACC at the bottom of the band flatters the enterprise value; a distress-consistent rate above it would lower the DCF and strengthen the conclusion.

On the base case the enterprise value is IDR1,077.6bn, with the terminal value carrying 46.0% of that figure. That is a low multiple of EBITDA on purpose: the conversion of EBITDA into free cash is poor because capex is close to D&A and working capital absorbs a fifth of every incremental rupiah of revenue. The bridge is struck entirely at 30 September 2026: it deducts borrowings of IDR4,159.0bn and lease liabilities of IDR1,335.0bn, adds back cash of IDR126.1bn and the investment stake of IDR199.7bn, and takes minorities from the same balance sheet [S14]. Lease liabilities enter as a separate deduction because the filing's own debt measure excludes them while our EBITDA is struck before lease depreciation and interest; the two lines together are the interest-bearing debt basis we use everywhere [S14]. Deducting that net debt and minorities and adding investments leaves a negative equity value, which the model floors at zero; the base-case target is therefore zero. This is not a rounding artefact: the enterprise would have to be worth several times our DCF value before shareholders kept anything.

The cross-check points the same way. At the peer median multiple of about six and a half times EBITDA the enterprise would still be worth less than net debt, and on any forward year we have modelled the same is true; the multiple test returns zero in every scenario the engine can run. The book-value anchor is the only measure that gives a positive number: book value per share was Rp68 at 31 December 2025 and Rp30 at our FY2026E balance sheet, falling to Rp-9 in FY2027E as losses consume equity. That book value includes the goodwill and intangibles created by the acquisitions that the DCF is effectively writing off, so we do not treat it as a floor.

What the price implies is the clearest way to state the call. At Rp118 the market capitalisation is IDR1,325.9bn; adding FY2027E net debt and minorities puts the enterprise at 17.7x our FY2027E EBITDA of IDR399.3bn [S14]. That is the forward-balance-sheet basis, it is the higher of the two, and it does not deduct the investment stake; on the printed 30 September 2026 bridge — net debt of IDR4,159.0bn plus IDR1,335.0bn less cash of IDR126.1bn, plus minorities and less the investment stake of IDR199.7bn — the same arithmetic against the same FY2027E EBITDA gives a multiple about three quarters of a turn lower, because FY2027E net debt is above the September figure. Against this year's lower EBITDA the same September bridge gives a higher multiple again. Whichever basis a reader takes, a rational buyer of a contract manufacturer earning a low-single-digit EBIT margin, with a capital-intensive asset base and customer concentration, would not pay that. The price embeds either a step-change in margin we cannot source or a willingness to underwrite the equity as a call option on a rescue.

The sensitivity grid is a statement in itself: because the enterprise value is a fraction of net debt, no discount rate or terminal growth in the plausible range moves the equity off zero. The operating grid, which flexes growth and gross margin a couple of percentage points either way, does not cross the debt line either. The equity becomes positive only under the much larger margin step-change in the bull case.

The dominant risk to our SELL is that we are wrong about the margin trajectory, not about the growth. If CDMO volume ramps faster than capacity and the current gross-margin gain continues, EBITDA could double from our base case and the equity would recover option value; we give that a real probability in the bull case rather than dismiss it [S8]. The company's own commentary points to exactly this path [S11].

The dominant risk to the share price, and the reason to avoid the name rather than simply dislike it, is refinancing. Interest-bearing borrowings of IDR4,159.0bn plus lease liabilities of IDR1,335.0bn against cash of IDR126.1bn at 30 September 2026 mean the group depends on rolling its facilities [S14]. The bond calendar is concrete: a series maturing in the first quarter of 2027, further series in 2028 and 2029, and a registered Phase II shelf bond of up to IDR650.0bn [S13][S14]. The group is already outside its debt-service and debt-to-equity covenants with no waiver disclosed [S14]. A refinancing on worse terms, or a covenant breach that forces an equity issue at a depressed price, transfers value from shareholders to lenders and new subscribers. Related-party risk is a live consideration given a controlling shareholder with a majority of the register [S15].

Operating risks are ordinary for the industry but material at this leverage: customer concentration in contract manufacturing, regulatory delays at either the Indonesian or the Australian site, and currency mismatch between rupiah costs and export revenue. On governance we can now be specific rather than cautious: the FY2025 accounts carry an unmodified opinion and disclose goodwill as the key audit matter [S16]; related-party balances are limited and no cash is placed with related parties [S16]; but the group's survival depends on a financial support letter from Rejuve dated 25 May 2026 that runs only to 1 June 2027 [S14]. Minority holders have little influence over capital allocation: the register is Rejuve at 60.5% and public holders below five per cent at 34.5% [S15], and only the 29.6% exchange free float actually trades, which is the figure the liquidity premium rests on rather than the public block.

The bear case slows volume, gives back the gross-margin gain and adds cost, so EBITDA stalls below cash interest, debt compounds and the equity is extinguished. The base case is described above: the business improves every year but never earns its cost of capital against this debt, and the equity is zero. The bull case accelerates CDMO contracts and lifts gross margin and cost absorption beyond the base, so EBITDA roughly triples and the enterprise crosses the debt line; it is the only state in which the equity has value, and it is worth Rp129 per share on our numbers, against 25.0% probability.

That asymmetry is the honest shape of this equity, and it replaces the earlier language about holders keeping a small stake. Neither the base nor the bear case delivers a residual; the bull delivers one without any new equity, because a bull that needed a rescue would not be a bull. The recapitalisation route does not restore value on its own: the registered Rights Issue II covers at most 5.7bn new shares, 33.65 per cent of post-issue capital, at an exercise price still left blank [S12], and at the 2024 precedent price that raises a sum well short of the equity deficit, so a subscribing holder would put in new money to own a larger share of an enterprise still worth less than its debt. That is why we do not model a raise as a source of per-share value.

We have sized the strategic route as far as the disclosure allows. The asset base — an Australian TGA-licensed contract manufacturer and an Indonesian formulation platform — is the kind of thing an international CDMO or a private-equity buyer would look at, and a trade sale is the one route to a positive equity value that our DCF does not capture. For the equity to be worth anything the enterprise must exceed net debt, minorities and investments; our DCF puts it at IDR1,077.6bn, so a buyer would have to pay several times that, which is a global-CDMO premium rather than an Indonesian formulator multiple. No approach has been disclosed [S14]. We flag it as the main upside risk to the call rather than build it into the base case.

Signposts that would change the view: a disclosed CDMO contract of a size that changes the revenue base; a gross margin sustained above the current level for two consecutive quarters; a completed equity raise large enough to cut net debt materially without wiping out existing holders; and any disclosure that separates CDMO revenue and margin from the legacy business [S8][S11].

Control sits with Rejuve Global Investment Pte Ltd, which held 60.5% of the register at 30 June 2026, while the public held 34.5% in blocks below five per cent [S15]. Those two figures are shareholder-register shares; the exchange's free-float measure of 29.6% is lower because it strips out the strategic holdings that sit inside the register, and it is that traded float, not the public register, that the small-cap premium in the valuation section is built on [S0][S15]. The group structure is a Singapore holding company over Indonesian operating subsidiaries and an Australian platform, acquired in stages: Holi Pharma, Ethica, Probiotec and the smaller service companies [S7]. That structure is normal for an Indonesian healthcare roll-up but it concentrates decision rights, and the acquisition programme itself was a related-party-sensitive use of capital.

The dividend record is empty: the group has paid no dividend while loss-making [S16]. That is the correct decision at this leverage and we do not treat it as a governance failure. What we watch is the opposite — any distribution, or any related-party transaction with the controlling shareholder's other interests, while the group funds a cash deficit with debt.

The audit opinion is unmodified and the key audit matter is the goodwill balance of 27.9% of consolidated assets [S16], which is the right thing for an auditor to test given the acquisition programme. We found no pledge of the controlling block disclosed in the filings we hold, and no special-monitoring-board status or special notation on the listing; that is a clean result from the search rather than a positive finding we can lean on. On ESG, the material exposure for a pharmaceutical manufacturer is environmental: effluent and solvent handling at formulation sites, and the energy intensity of the Indonesian plants. The company publishes a sustainability report alongside its annual report, but we could not retrieve its contents in this pass [S2].

The near-term catalyst is the audited FY2026 result, due by the end of the first quarter of 2027, which will show for the first time a full year of the current cost base and let us test whether the nine-month EBITDA run-rate held through the fourth quarter [S0]. Before that, the fourth-quarter trading statement and any refinancing announcement on the rupiah debt are the events that can move the equity, because the equity's value is a function of the debt terms rather than of the operating plan [S4].

Between updates we monitor four KPIs: quarterly revenue growth against the current rate; gross margin, which is the swing factor in the model; the split between EBITDA and finance cost, which tells us whether the group is closing the interest-coverage gap; and net debt, which tells us whether the operating improvement is being retained or borrowed away [S4][S11]. A CDMO contract announcement or a segment disclosure that separates contract manufacturing from the legacy business would be the single most useful piece of new information [S8].

The monitoring discipline matters more than usual here because our view is a balance-sheet view, and balance-sheet views are proved wrong by refinancing events rather than by quarterly earnings. If the group announces a facility extension on terms close to the current average, our interest assumption is too high and some equity value returns; if it announces a raise at a discount, the dilution is worse than we model. We would rather re-underwrite on that event than carry a range of outcomes that the disclosure does not support [S0].

bear.narrative: CDMO clients defer orders, the gross-margin recovery reverses toward the FY2025 level and fixed costs do not absorb; EBITDA stalls below cash interest, debt compounds and the equity is extinguished.

bull.narrative: The CDMO ramp at Probiotec and Ethica lifts gross margin toward the formulator peer range and fixed costs absorb as volume doubles; EBITDA roughly triples by the end of the decade and equity regains value without a rescue.

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 net revenue Rp2.41tn, +17.2% YoY, driven by CDMO/toll manufacturing at the Indonesian and Australian sites [S4]; Q4 2025 revenue Rp700bn implies FY2026E of about Rp3.2tn. Growth then fades with CDMO capacity absorption (Probiotec Australia, Ethica, Holi Pharma) rather than new acquisitions.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 gross margin 22.5% versus 20.3% a year earlier, with management attributing the gain to higher production volume spreading fixed costs [S4][S11]; FY2025 was 21.1% [S8]. We hold the 9M2026 level and add a modest absorption gain, not a price-driven expansion.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Total operating expense (including D&A) was 23.1% of 9M2026 revenue: gross profit Rp542.76bn less the Rp12.81bn operating loss gives Rp555.57bn of opex [S4]. FY2025 was 27.2% (Rp751.8bn on Rp2.76tn, S0). We assume continued fixed-cost absorption as CDMO volumes rise [S8].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: D&A was Rp292.7bn in FY2025 (10.6% of revenue) and Rp179.3bn in FY2024, mostly amortisation of the Probiotec acquisition intangibles [S16]; 9M2026 was Rp252.7bn, about 10.5% of revenue [S11]. The data pack carries only Rp96.8bn for FY2025, so history is restated from the filing. The charge fades with scale and converges to the capex rate by the terminal year, when the acquisition intangibles are fully amortised.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Cash capex was Rp168.3bn in FY2025 (fixed assets Rp139.4bn plus intangibles Rp28.9bn), 6.1% of revenue [S16], and Rp152bn over the LTM to June 2026 [S0]. We hold the last actual near term and then converge capex to the D&A charge (8% of revenue) by the end of the forecast: in a steady state a company cannot charge depreciation materially above reinvestment for ever, and the old 4% terminal rate left a permanent non-cash add-back that inflated terminal value.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital was Rp621.5bn, 22.5% of FY2025 revenue (S0), inflated by receivables from the acquired businesses; we hold that ratio rather than assume a release.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Indonesian statutory rate applied to a business carrying accumulated tax losses, so near-term cash tax is close to nil; we use the statutory rate rather than the loss-inflated effective rate in the 2025 accounts (S0).

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 finance cost was Rp322.43bn, which annualises to Rp429.9bn [S4]. The engine charges the rate on opening debt, so the rate that reproduces that run-rate on the corrected 31 Dec 2025 base of Rp4,841.4bn is 8.9% (429.9 / 4,841.4), giving Rp430.9bn for FY2026E rather than the Rp411.5bn a rate on average debt would imply; this replaces the earlier 8.5% that left the forecast below the filed nine-month charge. Part of the charge is non-cash - about Rp55.2bn of the nine-month figure is accretion added to lease liabilities [S14] - so the cash coupon rate is lower, near 7.5% of average debt, but the accrual charge the income statement shows is the right basis for interest cover and the loss path. New money is priced above the average: the Phase II 2026 shelf bond carries a 10.00-10.50% coupon [S13].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Cash of Rp130bn at 30 June 2026 (S0) earns a modest deposit rate well below the cost of debt in Indonesia; we use 4%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Interest-bearing debt was Rp4,841.4bn at 31 December 2025 (bank loans, bonds and lease liabilities) [S16] and Rp5,494.0bn at 30 September 2026 - Rp4,159.0bn of borrowings plus Rp1,335.0bn of lease liabilities [S14] - an increase of Rp652.6bn over nine months, four-fifths of the Rp804.6bn rise in total liabilities; the rest was payables, accruals and tax. Part of that increase never passes through cash: the 9M2026 lease note records additions of Rp35.6bn, accretion of Rp55.2bn and foreign-currency translation of Rp139.4bn, about Rp230.2bn of non-cash debt [S14]. The template debt line is cash-flow driven - debt is prior debt plus net borrowing and the same net borrowing is added to cash - so net debt moves only with the free-cash deficit and cannot carry that accretion. FY2026E net debt therefore lands about Rp240bn below the filed 30 September figure with no Q4 repayment assumed anywhere: the gap is the missing non-cash accretion, it understates leverage rather than flattering it, and the valuation bridge is struck at the filed 30 September balance sheet, so the target does not depend on it. Net borrowing equals the modelled cash burn each year, cash is held near the last actual, and the parent support letter of 25 May 2026 covers the Group until at least 1 June 2027 [S14].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Other income net of Rp11.09bn in 9M2026 versus a net expense in 9M2025 [S4]; treated as non-recurring and set to nil.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interests on the balance sheet are Rp215bn at 30 June 2026 (S0) but their share of profit is negligible in the reported P&L; we carry them in the bridge, not in the P&L split.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend has been paid while the group is loss-making and heavily levered (S0); we assume none through the forecast.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Shares outstanding are 11,236.69m at 31 Dec 2025 and 11,236.75m at 30 June 2026 [S0][S14]; the 30 September 2026 accounts report no outstanding dilutive potential ordinary shares, so the registered Rights Issue II [S12] is not yet effective and no new shares are in the base. Maximum registered size is 5.7bn new shares (33.65% of post-issue capital) with the exercise price still blank [S12]; at the 2024 precedent of Rp100 per share that raises about Rp570bn, far short of the equity deficit, so we treat the raise as a recapitalisation route in section 5, not as a source of per-share value.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Long-run Indonesian nominal GDP growth plus a small CDMO export contribution; below the house ceiling for IDR names and below the forecast growth fade.

challenges.challenge: The Rp0 target is a floor, not a value. All three scenarios return v0 = 0 and the WACC / terminal-growth sensitivity grid is zero in every cell, so the 45/30/25 probabilities have no effect and the -100% expected return is mechanical. Section 5 says the most likely path is 'a slow recapitalisation in which existing holders keep a small stake' and the bull case 'leave[s] a thin residual for equity', but the base case carries share_change 0 and net_borrowing tapering to 0 and values both states at zero. The base case does not model the path the report says is most likely.
challenges.answer: The base still values the equity at zero on operating value, but the scenario set is no longer degenerate: the bull carries a positive per-share value and the target is the probability-weighted result, not the floor. We removed the small-stake and thin-residual claims and quantified why the registered rights issue cannot close the deficit [S12][S14].

challenges.challenge: The price paragraph twice prints the market capitalisation as IDR1,325,936,438,994.0bn, which is 10^6 times the model's own mcap_rep of 1,325.9 IDR bn for 11,236.75m shares at Rp118. That is a Rp1.33 quadrillion market cap on Rp2.76trn of revenue, and it is the figure a reader must trust for the 17.4x claim.
challenges.answer: Both market-capitalisation prints now use the idrb filter and render Rp1,325.9bn on 11,236.7m shares; every other mkt money placeholder was checked and the one other money filter was removed from the prose [S16].

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA leg carries 50% weight but its metric is the FY2025A EBITDA line of -71.92, so it applies 6.5x to a negative historical number and returns an equity value of -5,938bn. Section 4 tells the reader it is '6.5x forward EBITDA', which the model never computed.
challenges.answer: The EV/EBITDA leg is removed from the blend because the engine applies the peer multiple to trailing LTM EBITDA, which was negative on the pack and still only Rp75.5bn restated; it is now a disclosed cross-check. The forward multiple quoted is the market own 19.0x on FY2027E EBITDA, labelled as the market multiple rather than the peer one [S16].

challenges.challenge: The post-balance-sheet review and its QC justification say the 9M2026 report is 'the one event of substance after the 30 June 2026 balance sheet' and that nothing goes into the bridge, but the analyst's own archived source S9 lists 'Abridged Prospectus for Capital Increase with Pre-emptive Rights II' and 'Abridged Additional Information on the Second Shelf-Registration Bonds of Pyridam Farma Phase II Year 2026'. Section 7 even lists any renewed equity-raising mandate as a catalyst while share_change is held at 0.
challenges.answer: Archived both documents as S12 and S13. The post-balance-sheet review now states their size, the blank exercise price and that neither is in the 30 September 2026 balance sheet, and the interim accounts report no dilutive instruments outstanding [S12][S13][S14].

challenges.challenge: The calibration BLOCK justification rests on 'on the same D&A basis FY2025A EBITDA is about Rp44bn'. The model's FY2025A line is EBIT -168.69 with D&A 96.76 (EBITDA -71.92); substituting the ~337bn annualised D&A the justification itself cites gives about +168, not +44. No source or arithmetic reconciles the two.
challenges.answer: History is restated line by line from the audited accounts: D&A Rp292.7bn, operating loss Rp217.2bn and EBITDA Rp75.5bn for FY2025, with Rp179.25bn, Rp106.88bn and Rp72.4bn for FY2024. The Rp44bn figure is withdrawn and the QC justification shows the arithmetic [S16].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the discount rate is 'pinned to the house band', but the model's WACC is 10.85% against the house IDR band of 11-13%, and the beta_levered of 1.79 is built from a config D/E of 2.0 rather than the company's actual gearing.
challenges.answer: WACC moved into the house band at 11.85% through a three-point small-cap cost-of-equity premium justified by a Rp1.33tn market capitalisation and a 34.45% float; section 4 now states that a higher, distress-consistent rate would lower the DCF and strengthen the call [S14][S15].

challenges.challenge: The report carries three net-debt figures: 4,738.5 in the thesis (FY2025A), 5,082.2 for FY2026E, and 5,255.8 in the valuation bridge, which is the 30 June 2026 balance sheet on a date the report never states. FY2026E debt of 5,341.4 is also below the June-2026 actual of 5,386.1, so the forecast assumes H2 2026 borrowing is negative while the cash path still starts from the FY2025A balance.
challenges.answer: One net-debt figure per date: FY2025A debt and cash restated from the audited liquidity note to Rp5,339.7bn and Rp101.8bn, the interim to Rp5,493.9bn and Rp126.1bn, and net borrowing is now the modelled cash burn so the forecast reconciles to the September balance sheet [S14][S16].

challenges.challenge: The report names a trade sale as 'the one route to a positive equity value that our DCF does not capture' and then leaves it out. It never shows the multiple at which equity becomes positive, which its own numbers put far above the 6.5x peer median and near the market's 17x - the number that decides the call. A TGA-licensed Australian CDMO site is priced by a strategic buyer on a different basis from an Indonesian formulator peer set.
challenges.answer: The strategic route is sized against the debt line: the report sets our DCF enterprise value against the net debt, minorities and investments a buyer must clear and says a buyer would have to pay several times it, which is a global CDMO premium rather than a formulator multiple; no approach is disclosed [S14].

challenges.challenge: S10 records that in 2024 PYFA completed a rights issue absorbing Rp1.07trn and issued Rp398bn of bonds, and section 6 says the controlling shareholder 'has injected capital before'. The report treats new equity only as dilution, never as the de-leveraging route that restores equity value; the 2024 precedent is archived and unused.
challenges.answer: The rights-issue route is quantified: maximum 5.7bn new shares, 33.65% of post-issue capital, exercise price left blank, and at the 2024 precedent price the proceeds fall well short of the equity deficit, so the raise is not a source of per-share value [S12].

challenges.challenge: Section 5 concludes 'the probability of an outright default is lower' and 'governance risk is moderate' with no covenant package, no maturity schedule, no bond coupon, no pledge status, no auditor opinion and no IDX board or notation check, and section 6 concedes the last two were not verified. Related-party flows are not quantified as a share of revenue anywhere in the report.
challenges.answer: Added the covenant package and the disclosed breach at both dates, the bond maturity calendar and coupons, the unmodified audit opinion with goodwill as key audit matter, the related-party position and the ownership split. The IDX board and notation status was searched and nothing was found [S14][S16][S15].

challenges.challenge: The report calls a dilutive raise 'high probability' and says it would 'transfer most of the residual equity to new money', but never sizes it: no amount, no price, no resulting per-share value. A rights issue priced below Rp118 leaves a holder who does not subscribe worse off than the model's zero - that is the actual bear case, and it is missing.
challenges.answer: Dilution is quantified in section 5: the registered maximum shares, the blank exercise price and the 2024 precedent show the raise cannot restore per-share value, and we no longer claim that existing holders keep a stake [S12].

challenges.challenge: The base case assumes share_change 0 and net_borrowing falling from 500 to zero while free cash flow after interest is negative and equity turns negative from FY2027E, with cash forecast negative by FY2029E. The DCF terminal FCFF also lets D&A run far above capex in perpetuity (2035 D&A about 502 against capex about 251), inflating a terminal value that is 59.1% of EV. Both need a source or an argument.
challenges.answer: Capex now converges to the D&A charge so terminal FCFF is on a maintenance-capex steady state, and net borrowing funds the modelled cash burn, holding cash at the last actual and showing debt rising to about Rp7.4tn by FY2030 instead of an open-ended overdraft [S14].

challenges.challenge: Fact F5 records FY2024 EBITDA of 71.6 (S10) while the model's FY2024A EBITDA line is 40.98 from the pack. The gap is never mentioned, even though the same pack-versus-company discrepancy is the entire argument for the FY2025 restatement.
challenges.answer: FY2024A is restated from the audited accounts to an operating loss of Rp106.88bn, D&A of Rp179.25bn and EBITDA of Rp72.4bn, consistent with the FY2025 treatment; the pack line of Rp41.0bn is withdrawn [S16].

challenges.challenge: The book-value anchor is quoted as 'Rp68 at the last accounts'. The last accounts are 30 June 2026 (equity 684.2 on 11,236.75m shares, about Rp61); Rp68 is the FY2025A equity. The one positive anchor in the valuation is overstated by roughly a tenth and cited to the wrong date.
challenges.answer: BVPS is now quoted by date: Rp68.3 at 31 December 2025 and Rp27.7 at our FY2026E balance sheet, with the negative FY2027E figure also shown rather than a single unlabelled number [S16].

challenges.challenge: Q10 stands and it is a model defect, not a typo. FY2026E debt 5,211.1 and net debt 5,109.3 sit Rp282.9bn and Rp258.6bn below the filed 30 September 2026 actuals of Rp5,494.0bn and Rp5,367.9bn [S14], and FY2026E finance cost sits below the Rp430bn implied by the 9M2026 Rp322.4bn [S4]. That implies an undisclosed Q4 2026 debt repayment of about Rp259bn, while section 3 says net debt rises with the modelled cash burn. A December 2026 balance sheet cannot be below a September 2026 filing without a sourced transaction.
challenges.answer: Interest is now 8.9% of opening debt, so FY2026E finance cost is 430.9 against the 429.9 implied by the 9M2026 322.43 annualised [S4]. No Q4 repayment is assumed anywhere: the shortfall against the filed 30 Sep figure is 230.2 of non-cash lease accretion (additions 35.6, accretion 55.2, AUD translation 139.4) that the template debt line cannot carry, and section 3 now reconciles it line by line [S14].

challenges.challenge: Q11a stands. Section 5 prints the registered Rights Issue II as at most IDR5.7bnbn new shares. That is the unit-error class that was FATAL C2 in the previous round; the correct figure is 5.7bn shares [S12].
challenges.answer: The rights issue now reads 5.7bn new shares, 33.65 per cent of post-issue capital, exercise price blank, from the PMHMETD II terms [S12]. A whole-document scan for a placeholder followed by a duplicated unit found no other instance.

challenges.challenge: Q11b stands. Section 5 says minority holders with 29.6 pct of the capital have little influence. 29.6 pct is the exchange free float; the register is Rejuve at 60.45 pct and public holders below five per cent at 34.45 pct [S15]. Calling the float the minority stake overstates the minority block and is the register conflation the business section correctly avoids two sections earlier.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now states the register, Rejuve at 60.45 pct and public holders below five per cent at 34.45 pct, as the governance block, and keeps 29.6 pct only as the exchange free float behind the liquidity premium [S15].

challenges.challenge: Q9 stands. The 17.6x is right on FY2027E net debt but the summary bullet and the price sentence both attach it to FY2027E EBITDA without saying so, while the printed 30 September bridge basis gives 16.8x. The later paragraph in section 4 does state the basis, so the defect is local, but the sentence a reader carries away is the one without the date.
challenges.answer: The 17.6x is now labelled FY2027E net debt and before the investment credit in the thesis and in the section 4 price paragraph, and the printed 30 Sep bridge is given with its components and a multiple about three quarters of a turn lower [S14]. The literal 16.8x cannot be typed under the placeholder law, so the bridge inputs are placeholders a reader can divide. The COE build now shows the default-spread subtraction and the beta multiplication and reconciles to 20.8% [S0].

missing_bull_case.note: The bull is only a +5pp growth / +1pp gross-margin shock and still floors at zero. The trade-sale route the report calls the main upside is never sized, and no calculation shows the EV/EBITDA at which equity becomes positive, so a reader cannot test the upside at all.

missing_bear_case.note: No covenant package, maturity schedule, bond coupon, pledge status, auditor opinion or IDX board/notation check, yet section 5 asserts outright default is 'lower' probability and governance risk 'moderate'; related-party flows are not quantified as a share of revenue.

assumption_realism.note: Opex/revenue falling from 22.7% to 20.5% carries more value than any other driver and is argued only from fixed-cost absorption. FY2026E debt of 5,341.4 sits below the 30 June 2026 actual of 5,386.1 and the cash path starts from FY2025A, so the forecast does not reconcile to the last balance sheet.

evidence_and_citations.note: S0 is cited for debt, cash, equity, the 29.6% float, the 70.1% insider block, employees and BVPS but is not archived in sources/; S7 carries no percentages. The market cap prints as IDR1,325,936,438,994.0bn, 10^6 too high. F5 (S10, FY2024 EBITDA 71.6) contradicts the model's FY2024A line of 40.98 and is never reconciled.

valuation_method_fit.note: The DCF family is right, but WACC 10.85% is below the house IDR band of 11-13% while section 4 says 'pinned to the house band'; the EV/EBITDA leg applies 6.5x to FY2025A EBITDA of -71.9 rather than forward EBITDA as the text claims; terminal FCFF carries D&A far above capex; and there is no implied exit versus entry multiple, ROIIC or fade statement.

bias_and_tone.note: Prose is disciplined and the call does not depend on a bearish operating view, but the conclusion rests on a floor: 'residual equity value is zero' contradicts section 5's 'existing holders keep a small stake' and the bull's 'thin residual for equity'. A rating that no probability can move is not being driven by the evidence.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The 6.5x peer median is reproducible from the PHARMA book (DVLA 6.8x, KLBF 6.0x) and the 17.4x FY2027E comparison uses the same convention as those peers; costs are IDR and the macro deck's rates flow through the WACC build. KAEF at 26x is the one outlier and does not move the median.

conservatism_audit.note: Departures that need sources: FY2025A restated EBITDA 'about Rp44bn' (the model's EBIT -168.69 plus the cited ~337 annualised D&A gives about +168, not 44); BVPS Rp68 quoted 'at the last accounts' against about Rp61 at 30 June 2026; 22% tax on a loss-maker; and a base case with no equity raise while the text calls one highly probable. Bear and bull shocks are mirrored, which is correct.

calibration.note: FY+1 does reproduce the 9M run-rate (17.5% growth on 9M +17.2%, 22.5% gross margin at the 9M actual), which is right. But the calibration BLOCK is justified on the unreconciled Rp44bn, the extreme_call is answered with '16x / EV 6.6tn' against the engine's 17.4x, reverse_dcf reports 'price not bracketed', and weights.changed is left unjustified.

signoff.notes: Approved. SELL and the Rp32 target survive every cross-check I have. The DCF enterprise is Rp1,077.6bn against net debt of Rp5,367.9bn at 30 September 2026 (borrowings ex-leases Rp4,159.0bn plus lease liabilities Rp1,335.0bn less cash Rp126.1bn), so equity is a residual floor at zero and the bridge, not the forecast line, carries that net debt. At the 6.5x peer median the enterprise would be about Rp2,595bn on FY2027E EBITDA of Rp399.3bn and still Rp2,773bn below filed net debt, so the call is not multiple-dependent; at a 10.0 pct WACC the enterprise is about Rp1,322bn and equity is still about negative Rp4,046bn, so it is not rate-dependent either. The 0/0/129 scenario set is non-degenerate, base 40 pct, and -72.6 pct is residual arithmetic on a levered CDMO, not a forecast of operational collapse: revenue grows every year and EBITDA rises. L1 is answered on substance: the gap between modelled FY2026E net debt and the 30 September filing is non-cash lease accretion (additions 35.6, accretion 55.2, AUD translation 139.4) disclosed line by line in section 3 [S14], not an undisclosed repayment; the direction understates leverage rather than flattering it, and the target rests on the filed bridge, so the conclusion does not move because equity is already zero. F39 is a FIX, non-blocking: it archives the 31 Dec 2025 lease liability as 1,334,966,814,196, a duplicate of the Sep column, where the S14 note shows 1,207,803,163,635, and no model line uses the Dec figure. Notes Q14/Q15/Q16 carry to the next version. No contamination.

bias.note: Base case anchored not cautious - revenue +17.5% vs 9M2026 actual +17.2% [S4], gross margin held at the 22.5% 9M rate [S4], D&A at the filed 10.5% [S11], capex and NWC at the FY2025 actuals [S16][S0]; the only large step (EBITDA margin 2.7% to 10.3%) is the 9M2026 run-rate of 10.0% (EBITDA Rp239.9bn on Rp2,410bn) annualised on FY2025 Q4 seasonality [S11][S4]. No drift flag fired. Scenarios mirrored on the same drivers (+/-5pp revenue growth, +/-5pp gross margin, -/+4pp opex); the bear probability of 35% against a bull 25% is supported by the disclosed covenant breach with no waiver and negative free cash flow before financing [S14]. The rating does not depend on the cautious DCF - at the 6.5x peer median (SIDO 6.5x, DVLA 6.8x) the enterprise is still below the Rp5,367.9bn filed net debt.

recomputed.item: Net debt rise 9M2026 (CFO 335.9 + CFI 65.9 + lease additions 35.6 + accretion 55.2 + FX 139.4)
FY2027E EV/EBITDA at Rp118 (mcap 1325.9 + net debt 5506.4 + minority 218.2 over EBITDA 399.3)

findings.finding: F39 archives the 31 Dec 2025 lease liability as 1,334,966,814,196, the same number as the 30 Sep 2026 column. The S14 lease note on page 71 gives the beginning balance at 1,207,803,163,635, and FY2025A total debt of 4,841.4 equals borrowings 3,633.6 [S14 comparative] plus leases 1,207.8 exactly. Only the 30 Sep 2026 figure feeds the bridge, so no model or report number moves, but the archived fact is wrong and a later reviewer will read the FY2025 lease balance as 127bn too high.

The 17.7x quoted in the thesis and section 4 is computed on modelled FY2027E net debt of 5,506.4, which carries the same omitted non-cash lease accretion that section 3 discloses for FY2026E (filed 9M accretion 55.2 plus FX 139.4 = 194.6 [S14]). The true FY2027E basis is therefore above 18x, so 17.7x is a minimum, not a point estimate.

Section 4 says the bridge takes minorities from the same balance sheet [S14]; the 218.2 is F29 from the FY2025 audited accounts [S16] (engine restated_bs period FY2025A), against 215.1 in the June 2026 pack. The 3.1bn difference cannot move a zero floor but the date label is wrong.

The WACC is built on a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.45% in the COC block while the interest calibration and the key input are 8.9%; at 8.9% the WACC would be about 11.6% rather than 11.85%. The direction is conservative, but a reader cannot reproduce 11.9% from the text.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves +7.6pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: FY2025A EBITDA is restated to Rp75.5bn: operating loss Rp217.2bn plus D&A Rp292.7bn from the audited statements [S16], not the pack's -71.9 which uses a Rp96.8bn D&A charge. The FY2026E margin of 10.3% is the 9M2026 actual run-rate - EBITDA Rp239.9bn on revenue Rp2.41tn, 10.0% [S11][S4] - annualised at the Q4 seasonality of FY2025. The step up from 2.7% to 10.3% is therefore an actual, not an assumption.

flags.message: ebit FY2024A restated at 3.65x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The pack's FY2024A EBIT of -29.2 is not the audited figure: the company reports an operating loss of Rp106.88bn for FY2024 and Rp217.2bn for FY2025 [S16], and the pack's D&A of Rp70.2bn against the filing's Rp179.25bn shows its opex scope for the Probiotec consolidation year is wrong. The pack computes EBITDA as a residual of a direct-method cash-flow statement; the audited income statement is authoritative, so history is restated line by line [S16].

flags.message: expected return -73%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The call rests on three sourced facts: finance cost of Rp322.43bn in 9M2026 against Rp239bn a year earlier [S4]; EBITDA of Rp239.9bn [S11], so cash interest exceeds EBITDA; and interest-bearing debt of Rp5,493.9bn at 30 September 2026 - Rp4,159.0bn of bank and bond borrowings plus Rp1,335.0bn of lease liabilities [S14] - against cash of Rp126.1bn, a net debt of Rp5,367.9bn. Our DCF enterprise value is far below that, so the equity is worth zero on the operating assets and the market price of Rp118 is paying for a recapitalisation or trade-sale option, not for cash flow.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'pe': 0.3, 'ev_ebitda': 0.1}
flags.justification: Weights are 100% DCF because neither multiple leg is a valuation method for this company: trailing EBITDA was negative on the pack and only Rp75.5bn restated [S16], and there are no earnings or dividends to support a P/E or yield. The peer EV/EBITDA cross-check is disclosed in section 4 rather than weighted, because any defensible multiple on FY2026E EBITDA leaves enterprise value below net debt.
